clinicalPearls: Typically affects adolescents and young adults, though it can occur at any age, without a strong sex predilection
Characteristically arises in para-articular deep soft tissue of the extremities, especially around the knee and thigh, but despite the name does not originate from synovium
Often presents as a slowly enlarging, sometimes long-standing and painful deep mass, which can lead to misdiagnosis as a benign lesion
Calcification within the tumour on imaging is a helpful, relatively characteristic feature

Defined by the t(X;18) translocation producing an SS18-SSX fusion gene (SSX1, SSX2, or less often SSX4), demonstrable by molecular testing and increasingly by SSX and SS18-SSX antibody immunohistochemistry
Morphology ranges from monophasic spindle cell to biphasic (spindle plus epithelial) and poorly differentiated patterns, with variable cytokeratin and EMA positivity
Local control relies on wide surgical excision, frequently combined with radiotherapy, and multi-agent chemotherapy is considered in selected higher-risk cases
A tendency to late local recurrence and metastasis, chiefly to lung, mandates prolonged follow-up
reference.pathophysiology: Synovial sarcoma is a translocation-associated malignancy of uncertain differentiation defined by fusion of SS18 on chromosome 18 with an SSX gene on the X chromosome. The resulting SS18-SSX fusion protein disrupts normal chromatin-remodelling complexes of the SWI/SNF (BAF) family, hijacking transcriptional programmes and derepressing target genes that drive proliferation and block normal differentiation. This epigenetic dysregulation, rather than any true synovial origin, underlies the tumour and its capacity for both spindle-cell and epithelial (biphasic) phenotypes; detection of the fusion is the diagnostic gold standard.
additionalDifferentials: Benign nerve sheath tumours and other slow-growing soft-tissue masses
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the primary site to assess deep extent and relation to joint and neurovascular structures
Plain radiographs to detect characteristic soft-tissue calcification
Chest CT for pulmonary metastatic surveillance
Whole-body functional imaging in higher-risk or large tumours
Core or open biopsy with careful tract planning and molecular testing for SS18 rearrangement
Immunohistochemistry including cytokeratins, EMA, TLE1, and SS18-SSX-specific antibodies
redFlags: A deep-seated, enlarging soft-tissue mass, especially near a joint in a young patient, wrongly labelled benign
A long-standing mass that begins to grow more rapidly or becomes painful
New respiratory symptoms suggesting pulmonary metastases
Recurrence at the primary site after apparently adequate excision
reference.prognosis: Outcome is influenced by tumour size, depth, grade, patient age, and adequacy of resection; smaller, completely excised tumours in younger patients fare better, but late recurrence and pulmonary metastasis are well recognised, so long-term survival can be worse than early results suggest.
pitfalls: Dismissing a deep soft-tissue mass as benign because of slow growth or long duration
Failing to obtain molecular confirmation of the SS18 fusion when morphology is ambiguous
Poorly planned biopsy that contaminates compartments and complicates limb-sparing surgery
Curtailing follow-up too early, missing late local or pulmonary recurrence
Interpreting focal keratin positivity in isolation without the full immunohistochemical and molecular context
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone
Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
management: Localized disease is managed with curative intent via a multimodality approach centered on surgery, while metastatic disease is treated with systemic therapy given the relative chemotherapy responsiveness of this subtype
Wide en bloc excision with negative margins, limb sparing where feasible, is the mainstay of local treatment, with excision of the prior biopsy tract as part of adequate surgery
Because the tumor can encase a major nerve, function sparing dissection is attempted, though nerve resection may be needed for high grade disease
Perioperative radiotherapy is considered for local control in high grade, deep, or large tumors or when margins are close or positive

Neoadjuvant or adjuvant chemotherapy, particularly ifosfamide based regimens such as an anthracycline plus ifosfamide combination, should be considered for high risk localized disease including high grade tumors over 10 cm or extremity disease of 5 cm or larger
Anthracycline monotherapy or an anthracycline based doublet may also be used perioperatively as a general soft tissue sarcoma approach

For metastatic or unresectable disease, first line systemic therapy favors an anthracycline plus ifosfamide combination when a response is needed, with single agent anthracycline as an option for patients with poorer performance status
Ifosfamide is noted as particularly active in this subtype
Later line options after anthracycline based therapy include gemcitabine plus docetaxel, single agent ifosfamide, pazopanib, dacarbazine, or trabectedin
Among tyrosine kinase inhibitors, pazopanib has shown modest activity while sorafenib, sunitinib, and mTOR inhibitors are not favored options in this subtype

Given expression of NY-ESO-1 and MAGE-A4, engineered T-cell receptor cellular therapies against these antigens are an emerging option with meaningful responses in early phase studies, and enrollment in clinical trials of novel or antigen directed agents is reasonable for advanced disease

Isolated or oligometastatic pulmonary recurrence can be managed with surgical metastasectomy, which is associated with prolonged survival, with repeat resection considered for further pulmonary recurrences in selected patients
Long term surveillance with primary site and chest imaging is needed well beyond the typical 5 year horizon due to a late recurrence pattern extending to 15 years

Management should be coordinated within a specialist sarcoma multidisciplinary team including surgical, radiation, and medical oncology from diagnosis, ideally before any biopsy or resection, with referral to a sarcoma trial center for advanced or refractory disease
